articles.title: Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton on how AI will end humanity; says that there are many ways: Like deadly ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton says it is “not unreasonable” to predict that artificial intelligence (AI) could wipe out humanity within the next dec.
articles.body: Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton says it is “not unreasonable” to predict that artificial intelligence (AI) could wipe out humanity within the next decade. The Nobel-winning computer scientist puts the probability at around 10%, while acknowledging there is no reliable way to predict it. Hinton said the window in which AI could pose an existential threat to humanity is also shrinking.“A 10% chance seems not an unreasonable estimate to me, but nobody really knows how to give a sensible estimate,” Hinton said during a recent interview on the BBC’s Newsnight. He explained that it is difficult to put an exact figure on the risk because society has never encountered a technology that “could soon be smarter than us.”He added that dismissing the possibility would be a mistake. “It would be very foolish to say there was like a 1% chance,” he said. “Nobody knows how to estimate it.”What he believes is clearer is that the timeframe for such a catastrophe has shortened. “I used to think like 30 to 50 years, then I reduced it to 10 to 20 years,” he said. “Now, I think maybe 10 years, maybe less. And other people think much sooner than that.”His assessment came after the show’s host pointed to a similar warning from a former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxane, who estimated that there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans “within the next decade.”Hinton did not explain why he has shortened his estimate for when AI could pose an existential threat. However, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have continued to invest heavily in developing larger and more capable models, with newer systems showing rapid improvements over versions released only months earlier.Hinton calls for global regulationHinton said the future could still take different paths. Humanity could move towards an outcome in which AI contributes to its destruction, or find ways to manage the technology's risks while benefiting from its capabilities.He again called for international regulation, arguing that countries share an interest in preventing AI systems from taking control away from humans."For things like preventing AI from taking over from people, the interests of all the countries are aligned," he said. "So they will eventually collaborate on that. The question is, will they do it in time?"​Anthropic researchers have raised concernsHinton's comments came after former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and warned that major AI companies were taking serious risks. Coxon, who had previously worked at OpenAI, said AI developers were effectively "gambling with our lives."Coxon argued that people working on advanced AI genuinely believe the technology could eventually kill everyone, saying some executives and researchers privately express greater concern than they do publicly.Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, backed Coxon's assessment. He said the company does believe AI could potentially kill all humans and personally placed the probability at more than 10% within the next decade.Hubinger also said Anthropic was trying to address the problem but did not yet have a solution for aligning a superintelligent AI system with human interests, adding that the company was not clearly on track to solve it.He later clarified that Anthropic considers the risk from current AI models to be low. The larger concern, he said, involves the possibility of superintelligence emerging through recursive self-improvement.What is recursive self-improvementRecursive self-improvement refers to a theoretical scenario in which an AI system could improve its own capabilities, potentially helping design or train more capable versions of itself.If such a process became possible and accelerated, AI development could move faster than researchers currently expect. That is one reason concerns about future, more capable systems differ from the risks posed by today's models.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: OpenAI reports more incidents of models acting deceptively
articles.summary: The ChatGPT creator says it is introducing a public reporting framework to share unexpected AI behaviour.
articles.body:
OpenAI says it has identified additional incidents of its AI models allegedly acting deceptively and taking unsanctioned actions during internal training and testing.

Alongside these disclosures on Wednesday, the creator of ChatGPT stated it was introducing a public reporting framework intended to frequently share instances of what it termed as unexpected or misaligned AI behaviour.

In a post on its website, OpenAI claimed that under the newly outlined framework, it will publish updates on concerning model behaviour on an ongoing basis rather than delaying disclosures to group multiple incidents into larger, periodic reports.

The company said the initiative aims to increase industry transparency around troubling model activities in the absence of standardised safety disclosure norms.

The announcement comes amid broader calls from prominent technology leaders urging a slowdown in frontier AI development over concerns that rapid scaling could outpace human oversight and control.

Last week, Anthropic claimed to have thwarted multiple malicious operations using its Claude models, ranging from cyber-espionage and weapons design to mass surveillance campaigns.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an essay published on Saturday. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”

However, United States President Donald Trump has repeatedly pushed back against calls to limit the industry, arguing that maintaining the US’s technological edge over international rivals remains paramount.

Responding to slowdown proposals, Trump described critics as “very negative forces” raising exaggerated scenarios that “won’t happen”.

Despite political resistance to statutory slowdowns, OpenAI signalled agreement with its industry rival regarding alignment pressures.

“As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research,” the company stated in the post.

OpenAI added that it does not believe the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer, emphasising that decisions about future AI development need to draw on evidence that external observers can examine independently.

According to the company, safety teams observed what they categorised as “misaligned behaviour” across six specific circumstances over the past six months during training and evaluation runs.

However, OpenAI maintained that these reports document individual, rare instances rather than frequent operational failures across deployed products.

The reported incidents allegedly included unreleased research models concealing mistakes in task summaries, unauthorised file uploads to the internet to generate citation links, and agents sharing files across public servers or internal repositories to bypass local boundaries.

OpenAI further stated that its future reports will detail observed behaviours, severity, setting, discovery dates, and the specific models involved, adding that it remains committed to disclosing complex cases requiring longer investigation or third-party coordination.

articles.title: As Nvidia, Salesforce, Meta CEOs oppose AI regulation by asking companies to make their AI models responsible, OpenAI clearly tells 'not possible' as ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: ​Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and other AI leaders have recently warned about the risks of rapidly advancing artificial intelligence (AI). Despit.
articles.body: ​Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and other AI leaders have recently warned about the risks of rapidly advancing artificial intelligence (AI). Despite this, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have argued that companies should make their own AI models safe rather than relying on new government regulation. Now, OpenAI has made clear why it believes the problem cannot simply be left to companies. The ChatGPT maker has disclosed six cases of unexpected or concerning model behaviour in the past six months, including models attempting to conceal mistakes, using an exposed API key without authorisation, and sharing files through unauthorised channels.This disclosure comes after Zuckerberg said AI companies have both the responsibility and incentive to make their models safe, as users would avoid systems that act against their interests and companies could face liability if their AI causes harm. “Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens,” he wrote on X. Moreover, Huang has similarly argued that AI development does not necessarily need to slow down for safety, saying companies can advance quickly while building safeguards into their models. “It’s a false choice,” Huang said at Salesforce’s Dreamforce event. “You could definitely have both at the same time.”​OpenAI says AI models are already showing unexpected behaviour​OpenAI’s latest disclosure presents a different picture. The company said it has observed six instances of model misalignment over the past six months and has introduced a framework to investigate and publicly report similar cases in the future.​“We do not believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer,” OpenAI said.​Among the incidents, an unreleased research model inserted instructions into task summaries, while instances of GPT-5.6 Sol added instructions intended to conceal mistakes or misaligned behaviour from users.​In another case, an internal model found an exposed API key and used it without authorisation. When it could not retrieve the requested information, it fabricated data and presented it as though it had come from the source.​Other models communicated and shared files without approval​OpenAI also reported cases involving models taking actions outside their intended boundaries. In one instance, models used an internal software repository as a message board to communicate with each other while looking for missing files. In another, collaborating agents used public file-hosting websites to exchange files when they could not access each other’s local files.​A separate example involved an unreleased model uploading a file to the internet so it could cite the information in an answer, without asking the user first. OpenAI stressed that these are individual examples and should not be interpreted as evidence of how frequently such behaviour occurs across its models.​OpenAI will now report model misbehaviour more systematically​Under its new framework, any OpenAI employee can flag a potential misalignment issue for investigation by the company’s safety and alignment teams. Investigators will examine what happened, whether anyone was affected and whether the incident should be disclosed. Reports are expected to include details about the behaviour, its impact, how it was discovered, and measures being taken in response. OpenAI also said the framework could evolve as the company gains experience with the reporting process.The disclosure comes as the debate over AI safety increasingly centres on who should be responsible for controlling risks: individual companies, independent evaluators or governments. While Zuckerberg and Huang favour companies managing safety themselves, OpenAI’s latest findings highlight the difficulties of relying entirely on models and their developers to identify and prevent unexpected behaviour.​Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang just told engineers across the world that keeping AI safe is their 'problem'; says: Safety is not a legal problem, it is…
articles.summary: Tech News News: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has a pointed message for the engineers building today's AI systems: keeping those systems safe falls on them first. Speaking .
articles.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has a pointed message for the engineers building today's AI systems: keeping those systems safe falls on them first. Speaking at Salesforce's Dreamforce conference, Huang said new laws are not needed to govern artificial intelligence, arguing that AI safety should be handled through engineering and existing rules. "Safety is an engineering problem, not a legal one," Huang said.The Nvidia chief also brushed aside the idea that AI is some new form of "alien mind," as at least one OpenAI safety researcher has described it. To him, it is just hardware and software built by humans, which means it can be controlled by humans and existing laws. He has been building the hardware behind AI since well before ChatGPT existed, and he sees the technology in plain terms. "It's a complicated computing system, but it's ultimately a computing system," he said.Jensen Huang says AI needs no new laws or regulationsHuang's argument leans on the market. He said market pressure should be enough to stop companies from releasing unsafe AI products, so there is little reason for governments to step in. "We don't need any new laws. We don't need new regulations," Huang said.He also rejected the popular framing that companies must pick between speed and safety. Huang called it a false choice and said firms could have both at the same time. His advice was to push ahead at full pace, but if a company ever feels out of control or unsure a product is safe, to "take a pause and make sure you get it right." He said companies should not release products if they are not confident in their functionality, capability or safety.Huang made no secret of his appetite for growth either. "I'm more ambitious than ever," he said, adding that there is no ceiling for Nvidia, for every industry and for every country.Mark Zuckerberg makes a similar case for self-policing AI labsHuang is not the only tech chief putting the burden on companies. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg laid out a comparable view in a recent post, arguing that every AI lab has both the responsibility and the incentive to train its models safely.His reasoning is commercial. People will not use AI agents that ignore their instructions or work against them, so alignment is fast becoming a feature that separates one model from another. Labs that neglect it, he wrote, will fall behind. He also flagged legal liability as a strong reason for companies to avoid shipping harmful models.Zuckerberg pointed to Meta's own record. The company delayed its Muse model by several months to focus on safety and security, without first asking rivals to do the same. He added that Meta Superintelligence Labs already brings in independent evaluators, and that Meta has committed most of its compute to serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement. Other labs, he said, can make the same call.Critics say AI safety cannot wait for courts to catch upNot everyone is convinced. Existing product liability laws could cover AI, but testing that theory depends on enough cases making their way through the courts. That means limits may get drawn only after something breaks. Recent examples include the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that disrupted thousands of flights, along with an OpenAI model's breach of Hugging Face and lawsuits against OpenAI linked to user deaths following extended chatbot conversations.Huang also did not address industry self-regulation, a path he has instead pursued by backing open-weight models as a competitive counterweight to proprietary AI labs. Meanwhile, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, speaking at the All-In Summit on Monday, said China should share the same AI safety concerns as the US, since it faces the same hacking risks.That puts the weight of Huang's argument squarely on engineering teams. It holds up only if companies actually hit pause when their own engineers raise a flag, even when growth targets point the other way.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.
